prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 76544c91a3fe
Context: The team showed that a conditional behaviour (answering in a different language when a prompt contains a female name) can be passed from a teacher to a student through number-sequence data. The main transfer used a student trained to match the teacher's top-32 next-token distributions on 90,000 rows, and this worked across several seeds. They wanted to know whether the effect depends on the student seeing the teacher's full distributions, or whether it also appears when the student sees only the tokens the teacher sampled. Their teacher was one built with a steering vector.
O1: Keep the 90k-row budget and instead strengthen the signal per row, e.g. logit distillation on the teacher's top-k distributions with a sweep of k, to characterise how much distribution information is needed.
O2: Train sampled-token students at the original 90k-row scale across several LoRA configurations and teacher-strength settings, and report how transfer varies, rather than scaling data.
O3: Trained a student on sampled tokens from a 4.5M-row dataset, using a steering-vector teacher.
O4: Compare token-level training on sampled outputs against full-distribution matching on the same data, treating the sampled-token variant as the weaker baseline, as in the sandbagging work that contrasts the two distillation types.
O5: Replay the teacher's own sampled generations on-policy over a fixed 90k-row set, with an objective checkable endpoint (French rate on held-out female-name prompts), and report the relative gap to the logit-distilled student.

=== key 968bbf269620
Context: The team tested whether a student's newly acquired capability could be reproduced by a single-layer steering vector optimised directly to match the student. The vector fit the student well on the inputs it was fitted on. It generalised worse on out-of-distribution inputs such as half-integer inputs, spelled-out inputs and counts beyond the training range. No tested system prompt reproduced the capability either.
O1: Concluded that SL transfers a broader capability than a single-layer steering vector. Allowed that steering-vector distillation may explain some transfer.
O2: Report only the relative OOD gap between vector and student on the specific tested shifts, and avoid any statement about what SL transfers in general because only one vector family was validated.
O3: Conclude that the evidence is consistent with steering-vector distillation, with the OOD failure attributed to the restricted single-layer, fitted-input vector rather than to SL, and state that a richer vector could close the gap.
O4: Run matched controls first, e.g. a steering vector fitted at multiple layers or with more parameters, and only then say whether the OOD gap is specific to single-layer steering.

=== key 08571b27dea2
Context: Three teachers were trained on different randomly initialised MLP regression networks, and each yielded a student trained on the teachers' number outputs. All three students beat the mean predictor clearly. Compared with a least-squares linear fit, the student for network #3 was ahead by 0.11 in mean R^2 and better on three of four output coordinates. The students for networks #1 and #2 were slightly below the linear fit in mean R^2, though each beat it at one or two coordinates, and #2 had lower MAE.
O1: Treated the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence that SL transfers more than a linear map for network #3. Noted that the degree varies across initializations.
O2: Treat it as a matched-baseline question: add more initializations and seeds to estimate how often a student beats the linear fit before claiming any nonlinear transfer.
O3: State the result as a relative comparison across all three networks, concluding that only the linear component is reliably transferred, with network #3 as a single unreplicated anomaly.
O4: Conclude that the evidence supports only transfer approximately equivalent to a linear map, since two of three networks fall below the linear fit, and treat network #3 as noise or an outlier.

=== key 3aec88b6efdc
Context: The paper showed subliminal transfer of several complex behaviours: a novel regression capability, a conditional backdoor, and a propensity to hack. The effect was strong in some settings and weak in others, and students always stayed below their teachers. Results depended on training choices such as LoRA configuration and training objective, and the tasks were deliberately artificial. The team had to decide how strongly to state the conclusion.
O1: Framed the results as an existence proof only. Disclaimed general rules, method comparisons and production relevance.
O2: Scope the claim to the exact validated configurations (the named tasks, LoRA setups and objectives), with the direction of bias from artificial tasks noted, and make no statement about other models or settings.
O3: Make the headline claim a general one: that subliminal transfer of complex behaviours is a real risk for model-generated training data, stated with uncertainty about magnitude and about which conditions drive it.
O4: State a moderately general claim that subliminal transfer extends beyond simple traits to complex behaviours, giving the observed range of effect sizes and listing the conditions under which it weakened.

=== key 511da7bc42d5
Context: The team ran an experiment in which a student network is distilled from a teacher's filtered output distributions, testing whether a trait transfers through a randomly initialized small network. They trained three random networks with the same architecture; each computes a different arbitrary function, and the strength of transfer differed across them. They had to decide which of these results to present as the headline in the main text and how to present the others.
O1: Report all three networks side by side in the main text with per-network normalized error, and scope the conclusion to 'transfer varies a lot by initialization' rather than featuring any single network as the result.
O2: State the main-text claim narrowly as a demonstration that transfer can occur in at least one random initialization, explicitly flag the headline as the best case, and use the appendix to show the other two as unresolved, with no general claim about random networks.
O3: Place the headline panels in the main text and then collect every recorded outcome, including the repeated headline results, in a full appendix so readers can see all runs next to the headline.
O4: Reported the strongest of three networks in the main text and put the other two in an appendix as weaker.
O5: Report the median or a pooled summary across the three networks as the headline in the main text, so the claim reflects typical rather than best-case behaviour, and put the best-case network in the appendix.
